Immigration and religion are deeply interconnected. Religion defies the concept that immigration is a one-time process defined at the point of entry or border. Rather, religious pathways create global ties and challenge the nation-state.[^1] This is because many immigrants come from countries where religion and culture overlap. When they reach their new home, they create diaspora communities while also contributing to their countries of origin in the form of remittances and social capital. Overall, Levitt argues that immigrants do not leave their religion behind; it is carried and evolves with them to create new transnational pathways. 

[^1]: Levitt, Peggy. God needs no passport. New York: The New Press, 2007.

Despite the religious diversity that frequently accompanies migration, specifically in the United States, scholars of both religion and migration have not taken an interdisciplinary approach to explore the relationship between the two variables.[^2] When the two variables are discussed together, they are often accompanied by xenophobic sentiments to promote anti-migrant rhetoric.

[^2]: Hagan, Jacqueline, and Helen Rose Ebaugh. "Calling upon the sacred: Migrants’ use of religion in the migration process." International migration review 37.4 (2003), 1145.

    \

The dataset I have chosen comprises the religious composition of the world’s migrant population from 1990 to 2020 as per the data collected by the United Nations Population Fund. Through this data story, I aim to explore the extent to which the religious composition of the world’s migrants has evolved from 1990 to 2020 through a data driven lens.

Religious familiarity is often sidelined as a factor influencing migration decisions. People often move to a different country to escape religious persecution or be around people who share the same religion. Zanfrini further explores how religion is often a push/pull factor when it comes to the decision of.[^3]

[^3]: Zanfrini, Laura. "On the role of religion in the decision to migrate." Migrants and religion: Paths, issues, and lenses. Brill, 2020, 315.

The choropleth map above illustrates the plurality of religions among incoming migrants in each country in 2020. In this context, plurality refers to the religion of the largest number of migrants in each country. The categories are Christian, Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist, Jew, Unaffiliated and Undetermined. This map enables the audience to visualise the geographical spread of migrants as per their religious categories. I allocated the "Undetermined" category to all the countries, especially smaller ones, where all religious groups were \< 10,000 people. As observed in the map, Christian migrants are the most numerous in the Americas and Europe. Whereas Islam is more prominent among migrants in North Africa and the Middle East. Hence, the map also reaffirms Zanfrini's theory that migrants are likely to migrate to countries that which have the same dominant religion as their own.

For this reason, Muslim immigrants tend to gravitate towards Saudi Arabia and Jewish immigrants have moved to Israel. When migrants do not have a religious affiliation or are Christians, the top destinations remain the United States, Russia and Germany (Kramer and Tong 11). Similarly, the strong presence of the Church plays a critical role in makesing Italy a desirable destination for Christian migrants from across the world.[^4] Overall, this school of thought reinforces that immigration patterns are not only determined by economic incentives but also sociocultural and religious affinities. 

[^4]: (Zanfrini 2020, 318)

Further, religion plays a critical role in all stages of the immigration process. Religion plays a critical role in the initial decision to migrate, where to migrate, the journey itself and integration into host societies (Hagan and Ebaugh 1146). In simpler words, a migrant’s entire immigration journey varies vastly depending on their religious affiliation, and they often use their religion during the process. For example, ethnic churches in Houston provide resources to members of their community to assist with resettlement (Hagan and Ebaugh 1155). This results in creating new communities away from home and creating communities on the basis of religious affiliation, which is often linked with their sociocultural identity. This creates a new sense of belonging for newly arrived immigrants to establish themselves in their host country while having the familiarity and support of their religious community and institutions. On the contrary, belonging to a minority religion makes seeking asylum and assimilating significantly harder. For example, the British immigration and asylum system is critiqued to be Islamaphobic and excludes Muslims from their definition of “British values and a British identity” (Migrants’ Rights Network). Religion is actively used by and against immigrants consistently throughout their journey.

In addition to playing a critical role in deciding which destination country to migrate to, religion is actively used by and against migrants consistently throughout their migration journey.

This series of pie charts encapsulates the total religious composition of the world’s migrants from 1990 to 2020 in five-year increments. This graph provides a basis for data story by illustrating that while the total number of migrants have nearly doubled from 1990 to 2020, the religious composition of the world’s migrants remains largely unchanged.
